# Builds

Source: https://docs.rs/about/builds

Docs.rs automatically builds documentation for crates released on [crates.io](https://crates.io/).
                It may take a while to build your crate, depending on how many crates are in [the queue](https://docs.rs/releases/queue).

                All crates are built in a sandbox using the nightly release of the Rust compiler.
                The current version in use is `rustc 1.98.0-nightly (c397dae80 2026-07-02)`.

                The README displayed on docs.rs follows Cargo’s `package.readme` rules.
                If `readme` is not set, docs.rs will look for `README.md`, `README.txt`, or `README` in the crate root.
                Set `readme = "path/to/file"` to use a custom file, `readme = true` to use `README.md`, or `readme = false` to disable the README.

                To recognize Docs.rs from your Rust code, you can test for the `docsrs` cfg, e.g.:

```
```
                To recognize Docs.rs from `build.rs` files, you can test for the environment variable `DOCS_RS`, e.g.:

`if var.is_ok `
              All targets other than `x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu` are cross-compiled. For implementation reasons, this is unlikely to change for the foreseeable future.

                You can configure how your crate is built by adding [package metadata](https://docs.rs/metadata) to your `Cargo.toml`, e.g.:

```
[]
 = ["--cfg", "my_cfg"]
```
`#[cfg(my_cfg)]` (not to be confused with `#[cfg(doc)]`) can be used for conditional compilation.
                This approach is also useful for setting
                When you start using docs.rs metadata or `#[cfg(docsrs)]` in your code, you might run into issues
                where your code builds fine locally but fails on docs.rs.
                To avoid this, you can add [ cargo docs-rs](https://github.com/dtolnay/cargo-docs-rs) to
                your test-suite.
                While it doesn't perfectly replicate our build environment, it can catch many common issues.

                The Docs.rs [README](https://github.com/rust-lang/docs.rs/blob/master/README.md#build-subcommand) describes how to build
                unpublished crate documentation locally using the same build environment as the Docs.rs build agent.

                Missing dependencies are a common reason for failed builds.
                Docs.rs dependencies are managed through
                [crates-build-env](https://github.com/rust-lang/crates-build-env).
                See [Forge](https://forge.rust-lang.org/docs-rs/add-dependencies.html) for how to add a dependency.

                Most of the sandbox is a read-only file system, including the source directory of your crate and its dependencies.
                If your `build.rs` generates files that are relevant for documentation, consider writing to the
                [cargo output directory](https://doc.rust-lang.org/cargo/reference/environment-variables.html#environment-variables-cargo-sets-for-crates),
                passed in the environment variable `OUT_DIR`.

All the builds are executed inside a sandbox with limited resources. The current limits are:

| Available RAM | 6.44 GB |
| Maximum rustdoc execution time | 15m |
| Maximum size of a build log | 102.4 kB |
| Network access | blocked |
| Maximum number of build targets | 10 |

                If your build fails because it hit one of these limits, please
                [open an issue](https://github.com/rust-lang/docs.rs/issues/new/choose)
                to get them increased for your crate.
                Since our build agent has finite resources, we have to consider each case individually. However, there are a few general policies:

If your crate fails to build for a reason not listed here, you can rebuild it from [crates.io](https://crates.io) website as you can see below:

Or you can [file an issue](https://github.com/rust-lang/docs.rs/issues) if you think it's a **docs.rs** issue.

# Metadata

Source: https://docs.rs/about/metadata

You can customize docs.rs builds by defining `[package.metadata.docs.rs]`
		table in your crates' `Cargo.toml`.

The available configuration flags you can customize are:

```
[]
 = "test"
[]
# Features to pass to Cargo (default: [])
 = ["feature1", "feature2"]
# Whether to pass `--all-features` to Cargo (default: false)
 = true
# Whether to pass `--no-default-features` to Cargo (default: false)
 = true
# Target to test build on, used as the default landing page (default: "x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu")
#
# Any target supported by rustup can be used.
 = "x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu"
# Targets to build (default: see below)
#
# Any target supported by rustup can be used.
#
# Default targets:
# - x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu
# - aarch64-apple-darwin
# - x86_64-pc-windows-msvc
# - aarch64-unknown-linux-gnu
# - i686-pc-windows-msvc
#
# Set this to `[]` to only build the default target.
#
# If `default-target` is unset, the first element of `targets` is treated as the default target.
# Otherwise, these `targets` are built in addition to the default target.
# If both `default-target` and `targets` are unset,
#   all tier-one targets will be built and `x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu` will be used as the default target.
 = ["aarch64-apple-darwin", "x86_64-pc-windows-msvc"]
# If you want to instead add another target without overwriting the default ones:
 = ["i686-apple-darwin"]
# Additional `RUSTFLAGS` to set (default: [])
 = ["--example-rustc-arg"]
# Additional `RUSTDOCFLAGS` to set (default: [])
 = ["--example-rustdoc-arg"]
# List of command line arguments for `cargo`.
#
# These cannot be a subcommand, they may only be options.
 = ["-Z", "build-std"]
```

# Shorthand URLs

Source: https://docs.rs/about/redirections

Docs.rs uses semver to parse URLs. You can use this feature to access
            crates' documentation easily. Example of URL redirections for
            `clap` crate:

| URL | Redirects to documentation of |
|---|---|
| [docs.rs/clap](https://docs.rs/clap) | Latest version of clap |
| [docs.rs/clap::Command](https://docs.rs/clap::Command) | Latest version of clap, and search for "Command" within the crate |
| [docs.rs/clap/~2](https://docs.rs/clap/%7E2) | 2.* version |
| [docs.rs/clap/~2.9](https://docs.rs/clap/%7E2.9) | 2.9.* version |
| [docs.rs/clap/2.9.3](https://docs.rs/clap/2.9.3) | 2.9.3 version (you don't need `=`unlike semver) |
| [docs.rs/clap/*](https://docs.rs/clap/*) | Latest version of this page (if it still exists). "latest" or "newest" work as well as `*`. |

# Download

Source: https://docs.rs/about/download

docs.rs stores the `rustdoc` output in a ZIP file.

                These archives can be used as a base for further processing of
                the documentation for offline readers like Dash or Zeal.
                **They are not directly usable for offline documentation.**

The download is possible for specific or semantic versions:

But also viaTo unpack the ZIP file you need any zip utility that supports PKZIP version 4.6 and BZIP2 & Deflate compression.

The archives will contain all the documentation HTML files for all targets and CSS/JS assets that are specific to the build. The default target will be found at the root, and other targets each in its own subfolder.

                Docs.rs is running rustdoc with `--static-root-path "/-/rustdoc.static/"`,
                which leads to all references to static assets breaking if they are not
                available under that path. Older builds used `--static-root-path "/"`, which
                means you will have to handle both.

                Since we're also adding `--emit=invocation-specific` to our build
                the archives will *not* contain any static assets that are specific to the
                toolchain. For now these will have to be downloaded file-by-file directly
                from docs.rs.

# Rustdoc JSON

Source: https://docs.rs/about/rustdoc-json

docs.rs builds & hosts the [ rustdoc JSON](https://doc.rust-lang.org/rustdoc/unstable-features.html#json-output) output.

This structured version of the documentation can be used for inspecting the docs and types of the crate in a programmatic way.

                The JSON file you're downloading might have been built with an older version of `rustdoc`
                so you might have to check the `format_version` attribute to determine how to parse the structure.
                The [ rustdoc-types](https://docs.rs/rustdoc-types/) crate helps with this.

**
                We started building rustdoc JSON on 2025-05-23. So any release before that won't have a download
                available until our rebuilds reached that release.
            **

                The download URLs can be generic or specific, depending on what you need. In case of rebuilds we
                also keep old format versions around. **Until we rebuilt all releases, we might return
                a `404 NOT FOUND` for some.**

By default we use `zstd` compression, which is more space efficient and faster to decompress. For more limited environments we also started supporting `gzip` compression. You can receive gzip by adding `.gz` to the given URL.

Here some URL examples you can use.

| URL | Redirects to JSON download of |
|---|---|
| [https://docs.rs/crate/clap/latest/json](https://docs.rs/crate/clap/latest/json) | latest version, default target, latest format-version |
| [https://docs.rs/crate/clap/latest/json.gz](https://docs.rs/crate/clap/latest/json.gz) | latest version, default target, latest format-version, gzip compression |
| [https://docs.rs/crate/clap/latest/json/42](https://docs.rs/crate/clap/latest/json/42) | latest version, default target, format-version 42 |
| [https://docs.rs/crate/clap/~4/json](https://docs.rs/crate/clap/%7E4/json) | latest v4 via semver, default target, latest format-version |
| [https://docs.rs/crate/clap/~4/json.zst](https://docs.rs/crate/clap/%7E4/json.zst) | latest v4 via semver, default target, latest format-version, zstd compression |
| [https://docs.rs/crate/clap/latest/i686-pc-windows-msvc/json](https://docs.rs/crate/clap/latest/i686-pc-windows-msvc/json) | latest version, windows target, latest format-version |

# palette - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/palette/0.7.6/palette/index.html

## Expand description

A library that makes linear color calculations and conversion easy and accessible for anyone. It uses the type system to enforce correctness and to avoid mistakes, such as mixing incompatible color types.

[§](https://docs.rs#where-do-i-start)Where Do I Start?

The sections below give an overview of how the types in this library work,
including color conversion. If you want to get your hands dirty, you’ll
probably want to start with [ Srgb](https://docs.rs/type.Srgb.html) or

[. They are aliases for the more generic](https://docs.rs/type.Srgba.html)

`Srgba`[type and represent sRGB(A), the most common RGB format in images and tools. Their documentation has more details and examples.](https://docs.rs/rgb/struct.Rgb.html)

`Rgb`The documentation for each module and type goes deeper into their concepts. Here are a few you may want to read:

- `Rgb`
- `Alpha`
- `convert`
- `cast`
- `color_difference`

[§](https://docs.rs#type-safety-for-colors)Type Safety for Colors

Digital colors are not “just RGB”, and not even RGB is “just RGB”. There are multiple representations of color, with a variety of pros and cons, and multiple standards for how to encode and decode them. Palette represents these “color spaces” as separate types for increased expressiveness and to prevent mistakes.

Taking RGB as an example, it’s often stored or displayed as “gamma
corrected” values, meaning that a non-linear function has been applied to
its values. This encoding is not suitable for all kinds of calculations
(such as rescaling) and will give visibly incorrect results. Functions that
require linear RGB can therefore request, for example, [ LinSrgb](https://docs.rs/type.LinSrgb.html) as their
input type.

[ⓘ](https://docs.rs)

```
// Srgb is an alias for Rgb<Srgb, T>, which is what most pictures store.
// LinSrgb is an alias for Rgb<Linear<Srgb>, T>, better for color manipulation.
use palette::{Srgb, LinSrgb};
fn do_something(a: LinSrgb, b: LinSrgb) -> LinSrgb {
// ...
}
let orangeish = Srgb::new(1.0, 0.6, 0.0);
let blueish = Srgb::new(0.0, 0.2, 1.0);
let result = do_something(orangeish, blueish); // Does not compile
```
The colors will have to be decoded before being used in the function:

```
// Srgb is an alias for Rgb<Srgb, T>, which is what most pictures store.
// LinSrgb is an alias for Rgb<Linear<Srgb>, T>, better for color manipulation.
use palette::{Srgb, LinSrgb};
fn do_something(a: LinSrgb, b: LinSrgb) -> LinSrgb {
// ...
}
let orangeish = Srgb::new(1.0, 0.6, 0.0).into_linear();
let blueish = Srgb::new(0.0, 0.2, 1.0).into_linear();
let result = do_something(orangeish, blueish);
```
See the [rgb](https://docs.rs/rgb/index.html) module for a deeper dive into RGB and (non-)linearity.

[§](https://docs.rs#color-spaces-and-conversion)Color Spaces and Conversion

As the previous section mentions, there are many different ways of representing colors. These “color spaces” are represented as different types in Palette, each with a description of what it is and how it works. Most of them also have two type parameters for customization:

- The component type (`T`) that decides which number type is used. The default is`f32`, but`u8`,`f64`, and any other type that implement the required traits will work. Including SIMD types in many cases.
- The reference white point (`W`) or standard (`S`) that affects the range, encoding or display properties of the color. This varies between color spaces and can usually be left as its default or be set via a type alias. For example, the`Srgb``LinSrgb``Rgb``S`) types.

Selecting the proper color space can have a big impact on how the resulting
image looks (as illustrated by some of the programs in `examples`), and
Palette makes the conversion between them as easy as a call to
[ from_color](https://docs.rs/convert/trait.FromColor.html#tymethod.from_color) or

[.](https://docs.rs/convert/trait.IntoColor.html#tymethod.into_color)

`into_color`This example takes an sRGB color, converts it to CIE L*C*h°, a color space similar to the colloquial HSL/HSV color spaces, shifts its hue by 180° and converts it back to RGB:

```
use palette::{FromColor, ShiftHue, IntoColor, Lch, Srgb};
let lch_color: Lch = Srgb::new(0.8, 0.2, 0.1).into_color();
let new_color = Srgb::from_color(lch_color.shift_hue(180.0));
```
[§](https://docs.rs#transparency)Transparency

There are many cases where pixel transparency is important, but there are
also many cases where it would just be unused memory space. Palette has
therefore adopted a structure where the transparency component (alpha) is
attachable using the [ Alpha](https://docs.rs/struct.Alpha.html) type. This approach has shown to be very
modular and easy to maintain, compared to having transparent copies of each
type.

An additional benefit is allowing operations to selectively affect the alpha component:

```
// Each color type has a transparent alias that ends with "a" for "alpha"
use palette::{LinSrgb, LinSrgba};
let mut c1 = LinSrgba::new(1.0, 0.5, 0.5, 0.8);
let c2 = LinSrgb::new(0.5, 1.0, 1.0);
c1.color = c1.color * c2; //Leave the alpha as it is
c1.blue += 0.2; //The color components can easily be accessed
c1 = c1 * 0.5; //Scale both the color and the alpha
```
There’s also [ PreAlpha](https://docs.rs/blend/struct.PreAlpha.html) that represents pre-multiplied
alpha (also known as alpha masked colors). It’s commonly used in color
blending and composition.

[§](https://docs.rs#images-and-buffers)Images and Buffers

Oftentimes, pixel data is stored in a plain array or slice such as a `[u8; 3]`. The [ cast](https://docs.rs/cast/index.html) module allows for easy conversion between Palette colors
and arrays or slices. This also helps when working with other crates or
systems. Here’s an example of how the pixels in an image from the

`image`
crate can be worked with as `Srgb<u8>`:```
use image::RgbImage;
use palette::{Srgb, Oklab, cast::FromComponents, Lighten, IntoColor, FromColor};
fn lighten(image: &mut RgbImage, amount: f32) {
    // RgbImage can be dereferenced as [u8], allowing us to cast it as a
    // component slice to sRGB with u8 components.
    for pixel in <&mut [Srgb<u8>]>::from_components(&mut **image) {
        // Converting to linear sRGB with f32 components, and then to Oklab.
        let color: Oklab = pixel.into_linear::<f32>().into_color();
        let lightened_color = color.lighten(amount);
        // Converting back to non-linear sRGB with u8 components.
        *pixel = Srgb::from_linear(lightened_color.into_color());
    }
}
```
Some of the conversions are also implemented on the color types as `From`,
`TryFrom`, `Into`, `TryFrom` and `AsRef`. This example shows how `from` can
be used to convert a `[u8;3]` into a Palette color, `into_format` converts
from  `Srgb<u8>` to `Srgb<f32>`, and finally `into` converts back from a
Palette color back to a `[u8;3]`:

```
use approx::assert_relative_eq;
use palette::Srgb;
let buffer = [255, 0, 255];
let srgb = Srgb::from(buffer);
assert_eq!(srgb, Srgb::<u8>::new(255u8, 0, 255));
let srgb_float: Srgb<f32> = srgb.into_format();
assert_relative_eq!(srgb_float, Srgb::new(1.0, 0.0, 1.0));
let array: [u8; 3] = srgb_float.into_format().into();
assert_eq!(array, buffer);
```
[§](https://docs.rs#a-basic-workflow)A Basic Workflow

The overall workflow can be divided into three steps, where the first and last may be taken care of by other parts of the application:

`Decoding -> Processing -> Encoding`[§](https://docs.rs#1-decoding)1. Decoding

Find out what the source format is and convert it to a linear color space. There may be a specification, such as when working with SVG or CSS.

When working with RGB or gray scale (luma):

-
If you are asking your user to enter an RGB value, you are in a gray zone where it depends on the context. It’s usually safe to assume sRGB, but sometimes it’s already linear.
-
If you are decoding an image, there may be some meta data that gives you the necessary details. Otherwise it’s most commonly sRGB. Usually you will end up with a slice or vector with RGB bytes, which can easily be converted to Palette colors:

```
use palette::{Srgb, cast::ComponentsAsMut};
// This works for any color type (not only RGB) that can have the
// buffer element type as component.
let color_buffer: &mut [Srgb<u8>] = image_buffer.components_as_mut();
```
- If you are getting your colors from the GPU, in a game or other graphical application, or if they are otherwise generated by the application, then chances are that they are already linear. Still, make sure to check that they are not being encoded somewhere.

When working with other colors:

-
For HSL, HSV, HWB: Check if they are based on any other color space than sRGB, such as Adobe or Apple RGB.
-
For any of the CIE color spaces, check for a specification of white point and light source. These are necessary for converting to RGB and other colors, that depend on perception and “viewing devices”. Common defaults are the D65 light source and the sRGB white point. The Palette defaults should take you far.

[§](https://docs.rs#2-processing)2. Processing

When your color has been decoded into some Palette type, it’s ready for
processing. This includes things like blending, hue shifting, darkening and
conversion to other formats. Just make sure that your non-linear RGB is made
linear first (`my_srgb.into_linear()`), to make the operations available.

Different color spaced have different capabilities, pros and cons. You may have to experiment a bit (or look at the example programs) to find out what gives the desired result.

[§](https://docs.rs#3-encoding)3. Encoding

When the desired processing is done, it’s time to encode the colors back into some image format. The same rules applies as for the decoding, but the process reversed.

- Okhwb with an alpha component. See the `Okhwba`implementation in`Alpha`
- [Oklaba](https://docs.rs/type.Oklaba.html)
- Oklab with an alpha component.
- [Oklcha](https://docs.rs/type.Oklcha.html)
- Oklch with an alpha component. See the `Oklcha`implementation in`Alpha`
- [Srgb](https://docs.rs/type.Srgb.html)
- Non-linear sRGB, the most common RGB input/output format.
- [Srgb](https://docs.rs/type.SrgbLuma.html)- Luma
- sRGB encoded luminance.
- [Srgb](https://docs.rs/type.SrgbLumaa.html)- Lumaa
- sRGB encoded luminance with an alpha component.
- [Srgba](https://docs.rs/type.Srgba.html)
- Non-linear sRGB with an alpha component.
- [Xyza](https://docs.rs/type.Xyza.html)
- CIE 1931 XYZ with an alpha component. See the `Xyza`implementation in`Alpha`
- [Yxya](https://docs.rs/type.Yxya.html)
- CIE 1931 Yxy (xyY) with an alpha component. See the `Yxya`implementation in`Alpha`

# lib.rs - source

Source: https://docs.rs/palette/0.7.6/src/palette/lib.rs.html

# palette/lib.rs

[1](https://docs.rs#1)//! A library that makes linear color calculations and conversion easy and
[2](https://docs.rs#2)//! accessible for anyone. It uses the type system to enforce correctness and to
[3](https://docs.rs#3)//! avoid mistakes, such as mixing incompatible color types.
[4](https://docs.rs#4)//!
[5](https://docs.rs#5)//! # Where Do I Start?
[6](https://docs.rs#6)//!
[7](https://docs.rs#7)//! The sections below give an overview of how the types in this library work,
[8](https://docs.rs#8)//! including color conversion. If you want to get your hands dirty, you'll
[9](https://docs.rs#9)//! probably want to start with [`Srgb`] or [`Srgba`]. They are aliases for the
[10](https://docs.rs#10)//! more generic [`Rgb`](rgb::Rgb) type and represent sRGB(A), the most common
[11](https://docs.rs#11)//! RGB format in images and tools. Their documentation has more details and
[12](https://docs.rs#12)//! examples.
[13](https://docs.rs#13)//!
[14](https://docs.rs#14)//! The documentation for each module and type goes deeper into their concepts.
[15](https://docs.rs#15)//! Here are a few you may want to read:
[16](https://docs.rs#16)//!
[17](https://docs.rs#17)//! * [`Rgb`](rgb::Rgb) - For getting started with RGB values.
[18](https://docs.rs#18)//! * [`Alpha`] - For more details on transparency.
[19](https://docs.rs#19)//! * [`convert`] - Describes the conversion traits and how to use and implement
[20](https://docs.rs#20)//!   them.
[21](https://docs.rs#21)//! * [`cast`] - Describes how to cast color types to and from other data
[22](https://docs.rs#22)//!   formats, such as arrays and unsigned integers.
[23](https://docs.rs#23)//! * [`color_difference`] - Describes different ways of measuring the
[24](https://docs.rs#24)//!   difference between colors.
[25](https://docs.rs#25)//!
[26](https://docs.rs#26)//! # Type Safety for Colors
[27](https://docs.rs#27)//!
[28](https://docs.rs#28)//! Digital colors are not "just RGB", and not even RGB is "just RGB". There are
[29](https://docs.rs#29)//! multiple representations of color, with a variety of pros and cons, and
[30](https://docs.rs#30)//! multiple standards for how to encode and decode them. Palette represents
[31](https://docs.rs#31)//! these "color spaces" as separate types for increased expressiveness and to
[32](https://docs.rs#32)//! prevent mistakes.
[33](https://docs.rs#33)//!
[34](https://docs.rs#34)//! Taking RGB as an example, it's often stored or displayed as "gamma
[35](https://docs.rs#35)//! corrected" values, meaning that a non-linear function has been applied to
[36](https://docs.rs#36)//! its values. This encoding is not suitable for all kinds of calculations
[37](https://docs.rs#37)//! (such as rescaling) and will give visibly incorrect results. Functions that
[38](https://docs.rs#38)//! require linear RGB can therefore request, for example, [`LinSrgb`] as their
[39](https://docs.rs#39)//! input type.
[40](https://docs.rs#40)//!
[41](https://docs.rs#41)//! ```rust,compile_fail
[42](https://docs.rs#42)//! // Srgb is an alias for Rgb<Srgb, T>, which is what most pictures store.
[43](https://docs.rs#43)//! // LinSrgb is an alias for Rgb<Linear<Srgb>, T>, better for color manipulation.
[44](https://docs.rs#44)//! use palette::{Srgb, LinSrgb};
[45](https://docs.rs#45)//!
[46](https://docs.rs#46)//! fn do_something(a: LinSrgb, b: LinSrgb) -> LinSrgb {
[47](https://docs.rs#47)//! // ...
[48](https://docs.rs#48)//! # LinSrgb::default()
[49](https://docs.rs#49)//! }
[50](https://docs.rs#50)//!
[51](https://docs.rs#51)//! let orangeish = Srgb::new(1.0, 0.6, 0.0);
[52](https://docs.rs#52)//! let blueish = Srgb::new(0.0, 0.2, 1.0);
[53](https://docs.rs#53)//! let result = do_something(orangeish, blueish); // Does not compile
[54](https://docs.rs#54)//! ```
[55](https://docs.rs#55)//!
[56](https://docs.rs#56)//! The colors will have to be decoded before being used in the function:
[57](https://docs.rs#57)//!
[58](https://docs.rs#58)//! ```rust
[59](https://docs.rs#59)//! // Srgb is an alias for Rgb<Srgb, T>, which is what most pictures store.
[60](https://docs.rs#60)//! // LinSrgb is an alias for Rgb<Linear<Srgb>, T>, better for color manipulation.
[61](https://docs.rs#61)//! use palette::{Srgb, LinSrgb};
[62](https://docs.rs#62)//!
[63](https://docs.rs#63)//! fn do_something(a: LinSrgb, b: LinSrgb) -> LinSrgb {
[64](https://docs.rs#64)//! // ...
[65](https://docs.rs#65)//! # LinSrgb::default()
[66](https://docs.rs#66)//! }
[67](https://docs.rs#67)//!
[68](https://docs.rs#68)//! let orangeish = Srgb::new(1.0, 0.6, 0.0).into_linear();
[69](https://docs.rs#69)//! let blueish = Srgb::new(0.0, 0.2, 1.0).into_linear();
[70](https://docs.rs#70)//! let result = do_something(orangeish, blueish);
[71](https://docs.rs#71)//! ```
[72](https://docs.rs#72)//!
[73](https://docs.rs#73)//! See the [rgb] module for a deeper dive into RGB and (non-)linearity.
[74](https://docs.rs#74)//!
[75](https://docs.rs#75)//! # Color Spaces and Conversion
[76](https://docs.rs#76)//!
[77](https://docs.rs#77)//! As the previous section mentions, there are many different ways of
[78](https://docs.rs#78)//! representing colors. These "color spaces" are represented as different types
[79](https://docs.rs#79)//! in Palette, each with a description of what it is and how it works. Most of
[80](https://docs.rs#80)//! them also have two type parameters for customization:
[81](https://docs.rs#81)//!
[82](https://docs.rs#82)//! * The component type (`T`) that decides which number type is used. The
[83](https://docs.rs#83)//!   default is `f32`, but `u8`, `f64`, and any other type that implement the
[84](https://docs.rs#84)//!   required traits will work. Including SIMD types in many cases.
[85](https://docs.rs#85)//! * The reference white point (`W`) or standard (`S`) that affects the range,
[86](https://docs.rs#86)//!   encoding or display properties of the color. This varies between color
[87](https://docs.rs#87)//!   spaces and can usually be left as its default or be set via a type alias.
[88](https://docs.rs#88)//!   For example, the [`Srgb`] and [`LinSrgb`] type aliases are both variants
[89](https://docs.rs#89)//!   of the [`Rgb`][rgb::Rgb] type, but with different standard (`S`) types.
[90](https://docs.rs#90)//!
[91](https://docs.rs#91)//! Selecting the proper color space can have a big impact on how the resulting
[92](https://docs.rs#92)//! image looks (as illustrated by some of the programs in `examples`), and
[93](https://docs.rs#93)//! Palette makes the conversion between them as easy as a call to
[94](https://docs.rs#94)//! [`from_color`][FromColor::from_color] or
[95](https://docs.rs#95)//! [`into_color`][IntoColor::into_color].
[96](https://docs.rs#96)//!
[97](https://docs.rs#97)//! This example takes an sRGB color, converts it to CIE L\*C\*h°, a color space
[98](https://docs.rs#98)//! similar to the colloquial HSL/HSV color spaces, shifts its hue by 180° and
[99](https://docs.rs#99)//! converts it back to RGB:
[100](https://docs.rs#100)//!
[101](https://docs.rs#101)//! ```
[102](https://docs.rs#102)//! use palette::{FromColor, ShiftHue, IntoColor, Lch, Srgb};
[103](https://docs.rs#103)//!
[104](https://docs.rs#104)//! let lch_color: Lch = Srgb::new(0.8, 0.2, 0.1).into_color();
[105](https://docs.rs#105)//! let new_color = Srgb::from_color(lch_color.shift_hue(180.0));
[106](https://docs.rs#106)//! ```
[107](https://docs.rs#107)//!
[108](https://docs.rs#108)//! # Transparency
[109](https://docs.rs#109)//!
[110](https://docs.rs#110)//! There are many cases where pixel transparency is important, but there are
[111](https://docs.rs#111)//! also many cases where it would just be unused memory space. Palette has
[112](https://docs.rs#112)//! therefore adopted a structure where the transparency component (alpha) is
[113](https://docs.rs#113)//! attachable using the [`Alpha`] type. This approach has shown to be very
[114](https://docs.rs#114)//! modular and easy to maintain, compared to having transparent copies of each
[115](https://docs.rs#115)//! type.
[116](https://docs.rs#116)//!
[117](https://docs.rs#117)//! An additional benefit is allowing operations to selectively affect the alpha
[118](https://docs.rs#118)//! component:
[119](https://docs.rs#119)//!
[120](https://docs.rs#120)//! ```rust
[121](https://docs.rs#121)//! // Each color type has a transparent alias that ends with "a" for "alpha"
[122](https://docs.rs#122)//! use palette::{LinSrgb, LinSrgba};
[123](https://docs.rs#123)//!
[124](https://docs.rs#124)//! let mut c1 = LinSrgba::new(1.0, 0.5, 0.5, 0.8);
[125](https://docs.rs#125)//! let c2 = LinSrgb::new(0.5, 1.0, 1.0);
[126](https://docs.rs#126)//!
[127](https://docs.rs#127)//! c1.color = c1.color * c2; //Leave the alpha as it is
[128](https://docs.rs#128)//! c1.blue += 0.2; //The color components can easily be accessed
[129](https://docs.rs#129)//! c1 = c1 * 0.5; //Scale both the color and the alpha
[130](https://docs.rs#130)//! ```
[131](https://docs.rs#131)//!
[132](https://docs.rs#132)//! There's also [`PreAlpha`][blend::PreAlpha] that represents pre-multiplied
[133](https://docs.rs#133)//! alpha (also known as alpha masked colors). It's commonly used in color
[134](https://docs.rs#134)//! blending and composition.
[135](https://docs.rs#135)//!
[136](https://docs.rs#136)//! # Images and Buffers
[137](https://docs.rs#137)//!
[138](https://docs.rs#138)//! Oftentimes, pixel data is stored in a plain array or slice such as a `[u8;
[139](https://docs.rs#139)//! 3]`. The [`cast`] module allows for easy conversion between Palette colors
[140](https://docs.rs#140)//! and arrays or slices. This also helps when working with other crates or
[141](https://docs.rs#141)//! systems. Here's an example of how the pixels in an image from the `image`
[142](https://docs.rs#142)//! crate can be worked with as `Srgb<u8>`:
[143](https://docs.rs#143)//!
[144](https://docs.rs#144)//! ```rust
[145](https://docs.rs#145)//! use image::RgbImage;
[146](https://docs.rs#146)//! use palette::{Srgb, Oklab, cast::FromComponents, Lighten, IntoColor, FromColor};
[147](https://docs.rs#147)//!
[148](https://docs.rs#148)//! fn lighten(image: &mut RgbImage, amount: f32) {
[149](https://docs.rs#149)//!     // RgbImage can be dereferenced as [u8], allowing us to cast it as a
[150](https://docs.rs#150)//!     // component slice to sRGB with u8 components.
[151](https://docs.rs#151)//!     for pixel in <&mut [Srgb<u8>]>::from_components(&mut **image) {
[152](https://docs.rs#152)//!         // Converting to linear sRGB with f32 components, and then to Oklab.
[153](https://docs.rs#153)//!         let color: Oklab = pixel.into_linear::<f32>().into_color();
[154](https://docs.rs#154)//!
[155](https://docs.rs#155)//!         let lightened_color = color.lighten(amount);
[156](https://docs.rs#156)//!
[157](https://docs.rs#157)//!         // Converting back to non-linear sRGB with u8 components.
[158](https://docs.rs#158)//!         *pixel = Srgb::from_linear(lightened_color.into_color());
[159](https://docs.rs#159)//!     }
[160](https://docs.rs#160)//! }
[161](https://docs.rs#161)//! ```
[162](https://docs.rs#162)//!
[163](https://docs.rs#163)//! Some of the conversions are also implemented on the color types as `From`,
[164](https://docs.rs#164)//! `TryFrom`, `Into`, `TryFrom` and `AsRef`. This example shows how `from` can
[165](https://docs.rs#165)//! be used to convert a `[u8;3]` into a Palette color, `into_format` converts
[166](https://docs.rs#166)//! from  `Srgb<u8>` to `Srgb<f32>`, and finally `into` converts back from a
[167](https://docs.rs#167)//! Palette color back to a `[u8;3]`:
[168](https://docs.rs#168)//!
[169](https://docs.rs#169)//! ```rust
[170](https://docs.rs#170)//! use approx::assert_relative_eq;
[171](https://docs.rs#171)//! use palette::Srgb;
[172](https://docs.rs#172)//!
[173](https://docs.rs#173)//! let buffer = [255, 0, 255];
[174](https://docs.rs#174)//! let srgb = Srgb::from(buffer);
[175](https://docs.rs#175)//! assert_eq!(srgb, Srgb::<u8>::new(255u8, 0, 255));
[176](https://docs.rs#176)//!
[177](https://docs.rs#177)//! let srgb_float: Srgb<f32> = srgb.into_format();
[178](https://docs.rs#178)//! assert_relative_eq!(srgb_float, Srgb::new(1.0, 0.0, 1.0));
[179](https://docs.rs#179)//!
[180](https://docs.rs#180)//! let array: [u8; 3] = srgb_float.into_format().into();
[181](https://docs.rs#181)//! assert_eq!(array, buffer);
[182](https://docs.rs#182)//! ```
[183](https://docs.rs#183)//!
[184](https://docs.rs#184)//! # A Basic Workflow
[185](https://docs.rs#185)//!
[186](https://docs.rs#186)//! The overall workflow can be divided into three steps, where the first and
[187](https://docs.rs#187)//! last may be taken care of by other parts of the application:
[188](https://docs.rs#188)//!
[189](https://docs.rs#189)//! ```text
[190](https://docs.rs#190)//! Decoding -> Processing -> Encoding
[191](https://docs.rs#191)//! ```
[192](https://docs.rs#192)//!
[193](https://docs.rs#193)//! ## 1. Decoding
[194](https://docs.rs#194)//!
[195](https://docs.rs#195)//! Find out what the source format is and convert it to a linear color space.
[196](https://docs.rs#196)//! There may be a specification, such as when working with SVG or CSS.
[197](https://docs.rs#197)//!
[198](https://docs.rs#198)//! When working with RGB or gray scale (luma):
[199](https://docs.rs#199)//!
[200](https://docs.rs#200)//! * If you are asking your user to enter an RGB value, you are in a gray zone
[201](https://docs.rs#201)//! where it depends on the context. It's usually safe to assume sRGB, but
[202](https://docs.rs#202)//! sometimes it's already linear.
[203](https://docs.rs#203)//!
[204](https://docs.rs#204)//! * If you are decoding an image, there may be some meta data that gives you
[205](https://docs.rs#205)//! the necessary details. Otherwise it's most commonly sRGB. Usually you will
[206](https://docs.rs#206)//! end up with a slice or vector with RGB bytes, which can easily be converted
[207](https://docs.rs#207)//! to Palette colors:
[208](https://docs.rs#208)//!
[209](https://docs.rs#209)//! ```rust
[210](https://docs.rs#210)//! # let mut image_buffer: Vec<u8> = vec![];
[211](https://docs.rs#211)//! use palette::{Srgb, cast::ComponentsAsMut};
[212](https://docs.rs#212)//!
[213](https://docs.rs#213)//! // This works for any color type (not only RGB) that can have the
[214](https://docs.rs#214)//! // buffer element type as component.
[215](https://docs.rs#215)//! let color_buffer: &mut [Srgb<u8>] = image_buffer.components_as_mut();
[216](https://docs.rs#216)//! ```
[217](https://docs.rs#217)//!
[218](https://docs.rs#218)//! * If you are getting your colors from the GPU, in a game or other graphical
[219](https://docs.rs#219)//! application, or if they are otherwise generated by the application, then
[220](https://docs.rs#220)//! chances are that they are already linear. Still, make sure to check that
[221](https://docs.rs#221)//! they are not being encoded somewhere.
[222](https://docs.rs#222)//!
[223](https://docs.rs#223)//! When working with other colors:
[224](https://docs.rs#224)//!
[225](https://docs.rs#225)//! * For HSL, HSV, HWB: Check if they are based on any other color space than
[226](https://docs.rs#226)//! sRGB, such as Adobe or Apple RGB.
[227](https://docs.rs#227)//!
[228](https://docs.rs#228)//! * For any of the CIE color spaces, check for a specification of white point
[229](https://docs.rs#229)//! and light source. These are necessary for converting to RGB and other
[230](https://docs.rs#230)//! colors, that depend on perception and "viewing devices". Common defaults are
[231](https://docs.rs#231)//! the D65 light source and the sRGB white point. The Palette defaults should
[232](https://docs.rs#232)//! take you far.
[233](https://docs.rs#233)//!
[234](https://docs.rs#234)//! ## 2. Processing
[235](https://docs.rs#235)//!
[236](https://docs.rs#236)//! When your color has been decoded into some Palette type, it's ready for
[237](https://docs.rs#237)//! processing. This includes things like blending, hue shifting, darkening and
[238](https://docs.rs#238)//! conversion to other formats. Just make sure that your non-linear RGB is made
[239](https://docs.rs#239)//! linear first (`my_srgb.into_linear()`), to make the operations available.
[240](https://docs.rs#240)//!
[241](https://docs.rs#241)//! Different color spaced have different capabilities, pros and cons. You may
[242](https://docs.rs#242)//! have to experiment a bit (or look at the example programs) to find out what
[243](https://docs.rs#243)//! gives the desired result.
[244](https://docs.rs#244)//!
[245](https://docs.rs#245)//! ## 3. Encoding
[246](https://docs.rs#246)//!
[247](https://docs.rs#247)//! When the desired processing is done, it's time to encode the colors back
[248](https://docs.rs#248)//! into some image format. The same rules applies as for the decoding, but the
[249](https://docs.rs#249)//! process reversed.
[250](https://docs.rs#250)
[251](https://docs.rs#251)// Keep the standard library when running tests, too
[252](https://docs.rs#252)#![cfg_attr(all(not(feature = "std"), not(test)), no_std)]
[253](https://docs.rs#253)#![doc(html_root_url = "https://docs.rs/palette/0.7.6/")]
[254](https://docs.rs#254)#![warn(missing_docs)]

[405](https://docs.rs#405)
[406](https://docs.rs#406)/// Checks if color components are within their expected range bounds.
[407](https://docs.rs#407)///
[408](https://docs.rs#408)/// A color with out-of-bounds components may be clamped with [`Clamp`] or
[409](https://docs.rs#409)/// [`ClampAssign`].
[410](https://docs.rs#410)///
[411](https://docs.rs#411)/// ```
[412](https://docs.rs#412)/// use palette::{Srgb, IsWithinBounds};
[413](https://docs.rs#413)/// let a = Srgb::new(0.4f32, 0.3, 0.8);
[414](https://docs.rs#414)/// let b = Srgb::new(1.2f32, 0.3, 0.8);
[415](https://docs.rs#415)/// let c = Srgb::new(-0.6f32, 0.3, 0.8);
[416](https://docs.rs#416)///
[417](https://docs.rs#417)/// assert!(a.is_within_bounds());
[418](https://docs.rs#418)/// assert!(!b.is_within_bounds());
[419](https://docs.rs#419)/// assert!(!c.is_within_bounds());
[420](https://docs.rs#420)/// ```
[421](https://docs.rs#421)///
[422](https://docs.rs#422)/// `IsWithinBounds` is also implemented for `[T]`:
[423](https://docs.rs#423)///
[424](https://docs.rs#424)/// ```
[425](https://docs.rs#425)/// use palette::{Srgb, IsWithinBounds};
[426](https://docs.rs#426)///
[427](https://docs.rs#427)/// let my_vec = vec![Srgb::new(0.4f32, 0.3, 0.8), Srgb::new(0.8, 0.5, 0.1)];
[428](https://docs.rs#428)/// let my_array = [Srgb::new(0.4f32, 0.3, 0.8), Srgb::new(1.3, 0.5, -3.0)];
[429](https://docs.rs#429)/// let my_slice = &[Srgb::new(0.4f32, 0.3, 0.8), Srgb::new(1.2, 0.3, 0.8)];
[430](https://docs.rs#430)///
[431](https://docs.rs#431)/// assert!(my_vec.is_within_bounds());
[432](https://docs.rs#432)/// assert!(!my_array.is_within_bounds());
[433](https://docs.rs#433)/// assert!(!my_slice.is_within_bounds());
[434](https://docs.rs#434)/// ```
[435](https://docs.rs#435)pub trait IsWithinBounds: HasBoolMask {
[436](https://docs.rs#436)    /// Check if the color's components are within the expected range bounds.
[437](https://docs.rs#437)    ///
[438](https://docs.rs#438)    /// ```
[439](https://docs.rs#439)    /// use palette::{Srgb, IsWithinBounds};
[440](https://docs.rs#440)    /// assert!(Srgb::new(0.8f32, 0.5, 0.2).is_within_bounds());
[441](https://docs.rs#441)    /// assert!(!Srgb::new(1.3f32, 0.5, -3.0).is_within_bounds());
[442](https://docs.rs#442)    /// ```
[443](https://docs.rs#443)    fn is_within_bounds(&self) -> Self::Mask;
[444](https://docs.rs#444)}
[445](https://docs.rs#445)
[446](https://docs.rs#446)impl<T> IsWithinBounds for [T]
[447](https://docs.rs#447)where
[448](https://docs.rs#448)    T: IsWithinBounds,
[449](https://docs.rs#449)    T::Mask: BoolMask + BitAndAssign,
[450](https://docs.rs#450){
[451](https://docs.rs#451)    #[inline]
[452](https://docs.rs#452)    fn is_within_bounds(&self) -> Self::Mask {
[453](https://docs.rs#453)        let mut result = Self::Mask::from_bool(true);
[454](https://docs.rs#454)
[455](https://docs.rs#455)        for item in self {
[456](https://docs.rs#456)            result &= item.is_within_bounds();
[457](https://docs.rs#457)
[458](https://docs.rs#458)            if result.is_false() {
[459](https://docs.rs#459)                break;
[460](https://docs.rs#460)            }
[461](https://docs.rs#461)        }
[462](https://docs.rs#462)
[463](https://docs.rs#463)        result
[464](https://docs.rs#464)    }
[465](https://docs.rs#465)}
[466](https://docs.rs#466)
[467](https://docs.rs#467)/// An operator for restricting a color's components to their expected ranges.
[468](https://docs.rs#468)///
[469](https://docs.rs#469)/// [`IsWithinBounds`] can be used to check if the components are within their
[470](https://docs.rs#470)/// range bounds.
[471](https://docs.rs#471)///
[472](https://docs.rs#472)/// See also [`ClampAssign`].
[473](https://docs.rs#473)///
[474](https://docs.rs#474)/// ```
[475](https://docs.rs#475)/// use palette::{Srgb, IsWithinBounds, Clamp};
[476](https://docs.rs#476)///
[477](https://docs.rs#477)/// let unclamped = Srgb::new(1.3f32, 0.5, -3.0);
[478](https://docs.rs#478)/// assert!(!unclamped.is_within_bounds());
[479](https://docs.rs#479)///
[480](https://docs.rs#480)/// let clamped = unclamped.clamp();
[481](https://docs.rs#481)/// assert!(clamped.is_within_bounds());
[482](https://docs.rs#482)/// assert_eq!(clamped, Srgb::new(1.0, 0.5, 0.0));
[483](https://docs.rs#483)/// ```
[484](https://docs.rs#484)pub trait Clamp {
[485](https://docs.rs#485)    /// Return a new color where out-of-bounds components have been changed to
[486](https://docs.rs#486)    /// the nearest valid values.
[487](https://docs.rs#487)    ///
[488](https://docs.rs#488)    /// ```
[489](https://docs.rs#489)    /// use palette::{Srgb, Clamp};
[490](https://docs.rs#490)    /// assert_eq!(Srgb::new(1.3, 0.5, -3.0).clamp(), Srgb::new(1.0, 0.5, 0.0));
[491](https://docs.rs#491)    /// ```
[492](https://docs.rs#492)    #[must_use]
[493](https://docs.rs#493)    fn clamp(self) -> Self;
[494](https://docs.rs#494)}
[495](https://docs.rs#495)
[496](https://docs.rs#496)/// An assigning operator for restricting a color's components to their expected
[497](https://docs.rs#497)/// ranges.
[498](https://docs.rs#498)///
[499](https://docs.rs#499)/// [`IsWithinBounds`] can be used to check if the components are within their
[500](https://docs.rs#500)/// range bounds.
[501](https://docs.rs#501)///
[502](https://docs.rs#502)/// See also [`Clamp`].
[503](https://docs.rs#503)///
[504](https://docs.rs#504)/// ```
[505](https://docs.rs#505)/// use palette::{Srgb, IsWithinBounds, ClampAssign};
[506](https://docs.rs#506)///
[507](https://docs.rs#507)/// let mut color = Srgb::new(1.3f32, 0.5, -3.0);
[508](https://docs.rs#508)/// assert!(!color.is_within_bounds());
[509](https://docs.rs#509)///
[510](https://docs.rs#510)/// color.clamp_assign();
[511](https://docs.rs#511)/// assert!(color.is_within_bounds());
[512](https://docs.rs#512)/// assert_eq!(color, Srgb::new(1.0, 0.5, 0.0));
[513](https://docs.rs#513)/// ```
[514](https://docs.rs#514)///
[515](https://docs.rs#515)/// `ClampAssign` is also implemented for `[T]`:
[516](https://docs.rs#516)///
[517](https://docs.rs#517)/// ```
[518](https://docs.rs#518)/// use palette::{Srgb, ClampAssign};
[519](https://docs.rs#519)///
[520](https://docs.rs#520)/// let mut my_vec = vec![Srgb::new(0.4, 0.3, 0.8), Srgb::new(1.3, 0.5, -3.0)];
[521](https://docs.rs#521)/// let mut my_array = [Srgb::new(0.4, 0.3, 0.8), Srgb::new(1.3, 0.5, -3.0)];
[522](https://docs.rs#522)/// let mut my_slice = &mut [Srgb::new(0.4, 0.3, 0.8), Srgb::new(1.2, 0.3, 0.8)];
[523](https://docs.rs#523)///
[524](https://docs.rs#524)/// my_vec.clamp_assign();
[525](https://docs.rs#525)/// my_array.clamp_assign();
[526](https://docs.rs#526)/// my_slice.clamp_assign();
[527](https://docs.rs#527)/// ```
[528](https://docs.rs#528)pub trait ClampAssign {
[529](https://docs.rs#529)    /// Changes out-of-bounds components to the nearest valid values.
[530](https://docs.rs#530)    ///
[531](https://docs.rs#531)    /// ```
[532](https://docs.rs#532)    /// use palette::{Srgb, ClampAssign};
[533](https://docs.rs#533)    ///
[534](https://docs.rs#534)    /// let mut color = Srgb::new(1.3, 0.5, -3.0);
[535](https://docs.rs#535)    /// color.clamp_assign();
[536](https://docs.rs#536)    /// assert_eq!(color, Srgb::new(1.0, 0.5, 0.0));
[537](https://docs.rs#537)    /// ```
[538](https://docs.rs#538)    fn clamp_assign(&mut self);
[539](https://docs.rs#539)}
[540](https://docs.rs#540)
[541](https://docs.rs#541)impl<T> ClampAssign for [T]
[542](https://docs.rs#542)where
[543](https://docs.rs#543)    T: ClampAssign,
[544](https://docs.rs#544){
[545](https://docs.rs#545)    #[inline]
[546](https://docs.rs#546)    fn clamp_assign(&mut self) {
[547](https://docs.rs#547)        self.iter_mut().for_each(T::clamp_assign);
[548](https://docs.rs#548)    }

[550](https://docs.rs#550)
[551](https://docs.rs#551)/// Linear color interpolation of two colors.
[552](https://docs.rs#552)///
[553](https://docs.rs#553)/// See also [`MixAssign`].
[554](https://docs.rs#554)///
[555](https://docs.rs#555)/// ```
[556](https://docs.rs#556)/// use approx::assert_relative_eq;
[557](https://docs.rs#557)/// use palette::{LinSrgb, Mix};
[558](https://docs.rs#558)///
[559](https://docs.rs#559)/// let a = LinSrgb::new(0.0, 0.5, 1.0);
[560](https://docs.rs#560)/// let b = LinSrgb::new(1.0, 0.5, 0.0);
[561](https://docs.rs#561)///
[562](https://docs.rs#562)/// assert_relative_eq!(a.mix(b, 0.0), a);
[563](https://docs.rs#563)/// assert_relative_eq!(a.mix(b, 0.5), LinSrgb::new(0.5, 0.5, 0.5));
[564](https://docs.rs#564)/// assert_relative_eq!(a.mix(b, 1.0), b);
[565](https://docs.rs#565)/// ```
[566](https://docs.rs#566)pub trait Mix {
[567](https://docs.rs#567)    /// The type of the mixing factor.
[568](https://docs.rs#568)    type Scalar;
[569](https://docs.rs#569)
[570](https://docs.rs#570)    /// Mix the color with an other color, by `factor`.
[571](https://docs.rs#571)    ///
[572](https://docs.rs#572)    /// `factor` should be between `0.0` and `1.0`, where `0.0` will result in
[573](https://docs.rs#573)    /// the same color as `self` and `1.0` will result in the same color as
[574](https://docs.rs#574)    /// `other`.
[575](https://docs.rs#575)    #[must_use]
[576](https://docs.rs#576)    fn mix(self, other: Self, factor: Self::Scalar) -> Self;
[577](https://docs.rs#577)}
[578](https://docs.rs#578)
[579](https://docs.rs#579)/// Assigning linear color interpolation of two colors.
[580](https://docs.rs#580)///
[581](https://docs.rs#581)/// See also [`Mix`].
[582](https://docs.rs#582)///
[583](https://docs.rs#583)/// ```
[584](https://docs.rs#584)/// use approx::assert_relative_eq;
[585](https://docs.rs#585)/// use palette::{LinSrgb, MixAssign};
[586](https://docs.rs#586)///

[591](https://docs.rs#591)/// assert_relative_eq!(a, LinSrgb::new(0.5, 0.5, 0.5));
[592](https://docs.rs#592)/// ```

[604](https://docs.rs#604)
[605](https://docs.rs#605)/// Operators for lightening a color.
[606](https://docs.rs#606)///
[607](https://docs.rs#607)/// The trait's functions are split into two groups of functions: relative and
[608](https://docs.rs#608)/// fixed/absolute.
[609](https://docs.rs#609)///
[610](https://docs.rs#610)/// The relative function, [`lighten`](Lighten::lighten), scales the lightness
[611](https://docs.rs#611)/// towards the maximum lightness value. This means that for a color with 50%
[612](https://docs.rs#612)/// lightness, if `lighten(0.5)` is applied to it, the color will scale halfway
[613](https://docs.rs#613)/// to the maximum value of 100% resulting in a new lightness value of 75%.
[614](https://docs.rs#614)///
[615](https://docs.rs#615)/// The fixed or absolute function, [`lighten_fixed`](Lighten::lighten_fixed),
[616](https://docs.rs#616)/// increase the lightness value by an amount that is independent of the current
[617](https://docs.rs#617)/// lightness of the color. So for a color with 50% lightness, if
[618](https://docs.rs#618)/// `lighten_fixed(0.5)` is applied to it, the color will have 50% lightness
[619](https://docs.rs#619)/// added to its lightness value resulting in a new value of 100%.
[620](https://docs.rs#620)///
[621](https://docs.rs#621)/// See also [`LightenAssign`], [`Darken`] and [`DarkenAssign`].
[622](https://docs.rs#622)pub trait Lighten {
[623](https://docs.rs#623)    /// The type of the lighten modifier.
[624](https://docs.rs#624)    type Scalar;
[625](https://docs.rs#625)
[626](https://docs.rs#626)    /// Scale the color towards the maximum lightness by `factor`, a value
[627](https://docs.rs#627)    /// ranging from `0.0` to `1.0`.
[628](https://docs.rs#628)    ///
[629](https://docs.rs#629)    /// ```
[630](https://docs.rs#630)    /// use approx::assert_relative_eq;
[631](https://docs.rs#631)    /// use palette::{Hsl, Lighten};
[632](https://docs.rs#632)    ///
[633](https://docs.rs#633)    /// let color = Hsl::new_srgb(0.0, 1.0, 0.5);
[634](https://docs.rs#634)    /// assert_relative_eq!(color.lighten(0.5).lightness, 0.75);
[635](https://docs.rs#635)    /// ```
[636](https://docs.rs#636)    #[must_use]
[637](https://docs.rs#637)    fn lighten(self, factor: Self::Scalar) -> Self;
[638](https://docs.rs#638)
[639](https://docs.rs#639)    /// Lighten the color by `amount`, a value ranging from `0.0` to `1.0`.
[640](https://docs.rs#640)    ///
[641](https://docs.rs#641)    /// ```
[642](https://docs.rs#642)    /// use approx::assert_relative_eq;
[643](https://docs.rs#643)    /// use palette::{Hsl, Lighten};
[644](https://docs.rs#644)    ///
[645](https://docs.rs#645)    /// let color = Hsl::new_srgb(0.0, 1.0, 0.4);
[646](https://docs.rs#646)    /// assert_relative_eq!(color.lighten_fixed(0.2).lightness, 0.6);
[647](https://docs.rs#647)    /// ```
[648](https://docs.rs#648)    #[must_use]
[649](https://docs.rs#649)    fn lighten_fixed(self, amount: Self::Scalar) -> Self;
[650](https://docs.rs#650)}
[651](https://docs.rs#651)
[652](https://docs.rs#652)/// Assigning operators for lightening a color.
[653](https://docs.rs#653)///
[654](https://docs.rs#654)/// The trait's functions are split into two groups of functions: relative and
[655](https://docs.rs#655)/// fixed/absolute.
[656](https://docs.rs#656)///
[657](https://docs.rs#657)/// The relative function, [`lighten_assign`](LightenAssign::lighten_assign),
[658](https://docs.rs#658)/// scales the lightness towards the maximum lightness value. This means that
[659](https://docs.rs#659)/// for a color with 50% lightness, if `lighten_assign(0.5)` is applied to it,
[660](https://docs.rs#660)/// the color will scale halfway to the maximum value of 100% resulting in a new
[661](https://docs.rs#661)/// lightness value of 75%.
[662](https://docs.rs#662)///
[663](https://docs.rs#663)/// The fixed or absolute function,
[664](https://docs.rs#664)/// [`lighten_fixed_assign`](LightenAssign::lighten_fixed_assign), increase the
[665](https://docs.rs#665)/// lightness value by an amount that is independent of the current lightness of
[666](https://docs.rs#666)/// the color. So for a color with 50% lightness, if `lighten_fixed_assign(0.5)`
[667](https://docs.rs#667)/// is applied to it, the color will have 50% lightness added to its lightness
[668](https://docs.rs#668)/// value resulting in a new value of 100%.
[669](https://docs.rs#669)///
[670](https://docs.rs#670)/// `LightenAssign` is also implemented for `[T]`:
[671](https://docs.rs#671)///
[672](https://docs.rs#672)/// ```
[673](https://docs.rs#673)/// use palette::{Hsl, LightenAssign};
[674](https://docs.rs#674)///
[675](https://docs.rs#675)/// let mut my_vec = vec![Hsl::new_srgb(104.0, 0.3, 0.8), Hsl::new_srgb(113.0, 0.5, 0.8)];
[676](https://docs.rs#676)/// let mut my_array = [Hsl::new_srgb(104.0, 0.3, 0.8), Hsl::new_srgb(113.0, 0.5, 0.8)];
[677](https://docs.rs#677)/// let mut my_slice = &mut [Hsl::new_srgb(104.0, 0.3, 0.8), Hsl::new_srgb(112.0, 0.5, 0.8)];
[678](https://docs.rs#678)///
[679](https://docs.rs#679)/// my_vec.lighten_assign(0.5);
[680](https://docs.rs#680)/// my_array.lighten_assign(0.5);
[681](https://docs.rs#681)/// my_slice.lighten_assign(0.5);
[682](https://docs.rs#682)/// ```
[683](https://docs.rs#683)///
[684](https://docs.rs#684)/// See also [`Lighten`], [`Darken`] and [`DarkenAssign`].
[685](https://docs.rs#685)pub trait LightenAssign {
[686](https://docs.rs#686)    /// The type of the lighten modifier.
[687](https://docs.rs#687)    type Scalar;
[688](https://docs.rs#688)
[689](https://docs.rs#689)    /// Scale the color towards the maximum lightness by `factor`, a value
[690](https://docs.rs#690)    /// ranging from `0.0` to `1.0`.
[691](https://docs.rs#691)    ///
[692](https://docs.rs#692)    /// ```
[693](https://docs.rs#693)    /// use approx::assert_relative_eq;
[694](https://docs.rs#694)    /// use palette::{Hsl, LightenAssign};
[695](https://docs.rs#695)    ///
[696](https://docs.rs#696)    /// let mut color = Hsl::new_srgb(0.0, 1.0, 0.5);
[697](https://docs.rs#697)    /// color.lighten_assign(0.5);
[698](https://docs.rs#698)    /// assert_relative_eq!(color.lightness, 0.75);
[699](https://docs.rs#699)    /// ```
[700](https://docs.rs#700)    fn lighten_assign(&mut self, factor: Self::Scalar);
[701](https://docs.rs#701)
[702](https://docs.rs#702)    /// Lighten the color by `amount`, a value ranging from `0.0` to `1.0`.
[703](https://docs.rs#703)    ///
[704](https://docs.rs#704)    /// ```
[705](https://docs.rs#705)    /// use approx::assert_relative_eq;
[706](https://docs.rs#706)    /// use palette::{Hsl, LightenAssign};
[707](https://docs.rs#707)    ///
[708](https://docs.rs#708)    /// let mut color = Hsl::new_srgb(0.0, 1.0, 0.4);
[709](https://docs.rs#709)    /// color.lighten_fixed_assign(0.2);
[710](https://docs.rs#710)    /// assert_relative_eq!(color.lightness, 0.6);
[711](https://docs.rs#711)    /// ```
[712](https://docs.rs#712)    fn lighten_fixed_assign(&mut self, amount: Self::Scalar);
[713](https://docs.rs#713)}

[736](https://docs.rs#736)
[737](https://docs.rs#737)/// Operators for darkening a color;
[738](https://docs.rs#738)///
[739](https://docs.rs#739)/// The trait's functions are split into two groups of functions: relative and
[740](https://docs.rs#740)/// fixed/absolute.
[741](https://docs.rs#741)///
[742](https://docs.rs#742)/// The relative function, [`darken`](Darken::darken), scales the lightness
[743](https://docs.rs#743)/// towards the minimum lightness value. This means that for a color with 50%
[744](https://docs.rs#744)/// lightness, if `darken(0.5)` is applied to it, the color will scale halfway
[745](https://docs.rs#745)/// to the minimum value of 0% resulting in a new lightness value of 25%.
[746](https://docs.rs#746)///
[747](https://docs.rs#747)/// The fixed or absolute function, [`darken_fixed`](Darken::darken_fixed),
[748](https://docs.rs#748)/// decreases the lightness value by an amount that is independent of the
[749](https://docs.rs#749)/// current lightness of the color. So for a color with 50% lightness, if
[750](https://docs.rs#750)/// `darken_fixed(0.5)` is applied to it, the color will have 50% lightness
[751](https://docs.rs#751)/// removed from its lightness value resulting in a new value of 0%.
[752](https://docs.rs#752)///
[753](https://docs.rs#753)/// See also [`DarkenAssign`], [`Lighten`] and [`LightenAssign`].
[754](https://docs.rs#754)pub trait Darken {
[755](https://docs.rs#755)    /// The type of the darken modifier.
[756](https://docs.rs#756)    type Scalar;
[757](https://docs.rs#757)
[758](https://docs.rs#758)    /// Scale the color towards the minimum lightness by `factor`, a value
[759](https://docs.rs#759)    /// ranging from `0.0` to `1.0`.
[760](https://docs.rs#760)    ///
[761](https://docs.rs#761)    /// ```
[762](https://docs.rs#762)    /// use approx::assert_relative_eq;
[763](https://docs.rs#763)    /// use palette::{Hsv, Darken};
[764](https://docs.rs#764)    ///
[765](https://docs.rs#765)    /// let color = Hsv::new_srgb(0.0, 1.0, 0.5);
[766](https://docs.rs#766)    /// assert_relative_eq!(color.darken(0.5).value, 0.25);
[767](https://docs.rs#767)    /// ```
[768](https://docs.rs#768)    #[must_use]
[769](https://docs.rs#769)    fn darken(self, factor: Self::Scalar) -> Self;
[770](https://docs.rs#770)
[771](https://docs.rs#771)    /// Darken the color by `amount`, a value ranging from `0.0` to `1.0`.
[772](https://docs.rs#772)    ///
[773](https://docs.rs#773)    /// ```
[774](https://docs.rs#774)    /// use approx::assert_relative_eq;
[775](https://docs.rs#775)    /// use palette::{Hsv, Darken};
[776](https://docs.rs#776)    ///
[777](https://docs.rs#777)    /// let color = Hsv::new_srgb(0.0, 1.0, 0.4);
[778](https://docs.rs#778)    /// assert_relative_eq!(color.darken_fixed(0.2).value, 0.2);
[779](https://docs.rs#779)    /// ```
[780](https://docs.rs#780)    #[must_use]
[781](https://docs.rs#781)    fn darken_fixed(self, amount: Self::Scalar) -> Self;
[782](https://docs.rs#782)}
[783](https://docs.rs#783)
[784](https://docs.rs#784)impl<T> Darken for T
[785](https://docs.rs#785)where
[786](https://docs.rs#786)    T: Lighten,
[787](https://docs.rs#787)    T::Scalar: Neg<Output = T::Scalar>,
[788](https://docs.rs#788){
[789](https://docs.rs#789)    type Scalar = T::Scalar;
[790](https://docs.rs#790)
[791](https://docs.rs#791)    #[inline]
[792](https://docs.rs#792)    fn darken(self, factor: Self::Scalar) -> Self {
[793](https://docs.rs#793)        self.lighten(-factor)
[794](https://docs.rs#794)    }
[795](https://docs.rs#795)
[796](https://docs.rs#796)    #[inline]
[797](https://docs.rs#797)    fn darken_fixed(self, amount: Self::Scalar) -> Self {
[798](https://docs.rs#798)        self.lighten_fixed(-amount)
[799](https://docs.rs#799)    }

[802](https://docs.rs#802)/// Assigning operators for darkening a color;
[803](https://docs.rs#803)///
[804](https://docs.rs#804)/// The trait's functions are split into two groups of functions: relative and
[805](https://docs.rs#805)/// fixed/absolute.
[806](https://docs.rs#806)///
[807](https://docs.rs#807)/// The relative function, [`darken_assign`](DarkenAssign::darken_assign),
[808](https://docs.rs#808)/// scales the lightness towards the minimum lightness value. This means that
[809](https://docs.rs#809)/// for a color with 50% lightness, if `darken_assign(0.5)` is applied to it,
[810](https://docs.rs#810)/// the color will scale halfway to the minimum value of 0% resulting in a new
[811](https://docs.rs#811)/// lightness value of 25%.
[812](https://docs.rs#812)///
[813](https://docs.rs#813)/// The fixed or absolute function,
[814](https://docs.rs#814)/// [`darken_fixed_assign`](DarkenAssign::darken_fixed_assign), decreases the
[815](https://docs.rs#815)/// lightness value by an amount that is independent of the current lightness of
[816](https://docs.rs#816)/// the color. So for a color with 50% lightness, if `darken_fixed_assign(0.5)`
[817](https://docs.rs#817)/// is applied to it, the color will have 50% lightness removed from its
[818](https://docs.rs#818)/// lightness value resulting in a new value of 0%.
[819](https://docs.rs#819)///
[820](https://docs.rs#820)/// `DarkenAssign` is also implemented for `[T]`:

[822](https://docs.rs#822)/// ```

[825](https://docs.rs#825)/// let mut my_vec = vec![Hsl::new_srgb(104.0, 0.3, 0.8), Hsl::new_srgb(113.0, 0.5, 0.8)];
[826](https://docs.rs#826)/// let mut my_array = [Hsl::new_srgb(104.0, 0.3, 0.8), Hsl::new_srgb(113.0, 0.5, 0.8)];
[827](https://docs.rs#827)/// let mut my_slice = &mut [Hsl::new_srgb(104.0, 0.3, 0.8), Hsl::new_srgb(112.0, 0.5, 0.8)];
[828](https://docs.rs#828)///
[829](https://docs.rs#829)/// my_vec.darken_assign(0.5);
[830](https://docs.rs#830)/// my_array.darken_assign(0.5);
[831](https://docs.rs#831)/// my_slice.darken_assign(0.5);
[832](https://docs.rs#832)/// ```
[833](https://docs.rs#833)///
[834](https://docs.rs#834)/// See also [`Darken`], [`Lighten`] and [`LightenAssign`].

[883](https://docs.rs#883)/// A trait for colors where a hue may be calculated.
[884](https://docs.rs#884)///
[885](https://docs.rs#885)/// See also [`WithHue`], [`SetHue`], [`ShiftHue`] and [`ShiftHueAssign`].
[886](https://docs.rs#886)///
[887](https://docs.rs#887)/// ```
[888](https://docs.rs#888)/// use approx::assert_relative_eq;
[889](https://docs.rs#889)/// use palette::{GetHue, LinSrgb};
[890](https://docs.rs#890)///
[891](https://docs.rs#891)/// let red = LinSrgb::new(1.0f32, 0.0, 0.0);
[892](https://docs.rs#892)/// let green = LinSrgb::new(0.0f32, 1.0, 0.0);
[893](https://docs.rs#893)/// let blue = LinSrgb::new(0.0f32, 0.0, 1.0);
[894](https://docs.rs#894)/// let gray = LinSrgb::new(0.5f32, 0.5, 0.5);
[895](https://docs.rs#895)///
[896](https://docs.rs#896)/// assert_relative_eq!(red.get_hue(), 0.0.into());
[897](https://docs.rs#897)/// assert_relative_eq!(green.get_hue(), 120.0.into());
[898](https://docs.rs#898)/// assert_relative_eq!(blue.get_hue(), 240.0.into());
[899](https://docs.rs#899)/// assert_relative_eq!(gray.get_hue(), 0.0.into());
[900](https://docs.rs#900)/// ```
[901](https://docs.rs#901)pub trait GetHue {
[902](https://docs.rs#902)    /// The kind of hue unit this color space uses.
[903](https://docs.rs#903)    ///
[904](https://docs.rs#904)    /// The hue is most commonly calculated as an angle around a color circle
[905](https://docs.rs#905)    /// and may not always be uniform between color spaces. It's therefore not
[906](https://docs.rs#906)    /// recommended to take one type of hue and apply it to a color space that
[907](https://docs.rs#907)    /// expects an other.
[908](https://docs.rs#908)    type Hue;
[909](https://docs.rs#909)
[910](https://docs.rs#910)    /// Calculate a hue if possible.
[911](https://docs.rs#911)    ///
[912](https://docs.rs#912)    /// Colors in the gray scale has no well defined hue and should preferably
[913](https://docs.rs#913)    /// return `0`.
[914](https://docs.rs#914)    #[must_use]
[915](https://docs.rs#915)    fn get_hue(&self) -> Self::Hue;
[916](https://docs.rs#916)}
[917](https://docs.rs#917)
[918](https://docs.rs#918)/// Change the hue of a color to a specific value.
[919](https://docs.rs#919)///
[920](https://docs.rs#920)/// See also [`SetHue`], [`GetHue`], [`ShiftHue`] and [`ShiftHueAssign`].
[921](https://docs.rs#921)///
[922](https://docs.rs#922)/// ```
[923](https://docs.rs#923)/// use palette::{Hsl, WithHue};
[924](https://docs.rs#924)///
[925](https://docs.rs#925)/// let green = Hsl::new_srgb(120.0, 1.0, 0.5);
[926](https://docs.rs#926)/// let blue = green.with_hue(240.0);
[927](https://docs.rs#927)/// assert_eq!(blue, Hsl::new_srgb(240.0, 1.0, 0.5));
[928](https://docs.rs#928)/// ```
[929](https://docs.rs#929)pub trait WithHue<H> {
[930](https://docs.rs#930)    /// Return a copy of `self` with a specific hue.
[931](https://docs.rs#931)    #[must_use]

[933](https://docs.rs#933)}
[934](https://docs.rs#934)
[935](https://docs.rs#935)/// Change the hue of a color to a specific value without moving.

[944](https://docs.rs#944)/// assert_eq!(color, Hsl::new_srgb(240.0, 1.0, 0.5));

[950](https://docs.rs#950)/// use palette::{Hsl, SetHue};
[951](https://docs.rs#951)///
[952](https://docs.rs#952)/// let mut my_vec = vec![Hsl::new_srgb(104.0, 0.3, 0.8), Hsl::new_srgb(113.0, 0.5, 0.8)];
[953](https://docs.rs#953)/// let mut my_array = [Hsl::new_srgb(104.0, 0.3, 0.8), Hsl::new_srgb(113.0, 0.5, 0.8)];

[997](https://docs.rs#997)/// Assigning operator for increasing or decreasing the hue by an amount.

[1009](https://docs.rs#1009)/// `ShiftHueAssign` is also implemented for `[T]`:

[1012](https://docs.rs#1012)/// use palette::{Hsl, ShiftHueAssign};

[1044](https://docs.rs#1044)/// Operator for increasing the saturation (or chroma) of a color.
[1045](https://docs.rs#1045)///
[1046](https://docs.rs#1046)/// The trait's functions are split into two groups of functions: relative and
[1047](https://docs.rs#1047)/// fixed/absolute.
[1048](https://docs.rs#1048)///
[1049](https://docs.rs#1049)/// The relative function, [`saturate`](Saturate::saturate), scales the
[1050](https://docs.rs#1050)/// saturation towards the maximum saturation value. This means that for a color
[1051](https://docs.rs#1051)/// with 50% saturation, if `saturate(0.5)` is applied to it, the color will
[1052](https://docs.rs#1052)/// scale halfway to the maximum value of 100% resulting in a new saturation
[1053](https://docs.rs#1053)/// value of 75%.
[1054](https://docs.rs#1054)///
[1055](https://docs.rs#1055)/// The fixed or absolute function,
[1056](https://docs.rs#1056)/// [`saturate_fixed`](Saturate::saturate_fixed), increases the saturation by an
[1057](https://docs.rs#1057)/// amount that is independent of the current saturation of the color. So for a
[1058](https://docs.rs#1058)/// color with 50% saturation, if `saturate_fixed(0.5)` is applied to it, the
[1059](https://docs.rs#1059)/// color will have 50% saturation added to its saturation value resulting in a
[1060](https://docs.rs#1060)/// new value of 100%.
[1061](https://docs.rs#1061)///
[1062](https://docs.rs#1062)/// See also [`SaturateAssign`], [`Desaturate`] and [`DesaturateAssign`].
[1063](https://docs.rs#1063)///
[1064](https://docs.rs#1064)/// ```
[1065](https://docs.rs#1065)/// use approx::assert_relative_eq;
[1066](https://docs.rs#1066)/// use palette::{Hsv, Saturate};
[1067](https://docs.rs#1067)///
[1068](https://docs.rs#1068)/// let a = Hsv::new_srgb(0.0, 0.5, 1.0);
[1069](https://docs.rs#1069)///
[1070](https://docs.rs#1070)/// assert_relative_eq!(a.saturate(0.5).saturation, 0.75);
[1071](https://docs.rs#1071)/// assert_relative_eq!(a.saturate_fixed(0.5).saturation, 1.0);
[1072](https://docs.rs#1072)/// ```
[1073](https://docs.rs#1073)pub trait Saturate {
[1074](https://docs.rs#1074)    /// The type of the saturation modifier.
[1075](https://docs.rs#1075)    type Scalar;
[1076](https://docs.rs#1076)
[1077](https://docs.rs#1077)    /// Scale the color towards the maximum saturation by `factor`, a value
[1078](https://docs.rs#1078)    /// ranging from `0.0` to `1.0`.
[1079](https://docs.rs#1079)    ///
[1080](https://docs.rs#1080)    /// ```
[1081](https://docs.rs#1081)    /// use approx::assert_relative_eq;
[1082](https://docs.rs#1082)    /// use palette::{Hsl, Saturate};
[1083](https://docs.rs#1083)    ///
[1084](https://docs.rs#1084)    /// let color = Hsl::new_srgb(0.0, 0.5, 0.5);
[1085](https://docs.rs#1085)    /// assert_relative_eq!(color.saturate(0.5).saturation, 0.75);
[1086](https://docs.rs#1086)    /// ```
[1087](https://docs.rs#1087)    #[must_use]
[1088](https://docs.rs#1088)    fn saturate(self, factor: Self::Scalar) -> Self;
[1089](https://docs.rs#1089)
[1090](https://docs.rs#1090)    /// Increase the saturation by `amount`, a value ranging from `0.0` to
[1091](https://docs.rs#1091)    /// `1.0`.
[1092](https://docs.rs#1092)    ///
[1093](https://docs.rs#1093)    /// ```
[1094](https://docs.rs#1094)    /// use approx::assert_relative_eq;
[1095](https://docs.rs#1095)    /// use palette::{Hsl, Saturate};
[1096](https://docs.rs#1096)    ///
[1097](https://docs.rs#1097)    /// let color = Hsl::new_srgb(0.0, 0.4, 0.5);
[1098](https://docs.rs#1098)    /// assert_relative_eq!(color.saturate_fixed(0.2).saturation, 0.6);
[1099](https://docs.rs#1099)    /// ```
[1100](https://docs.rs#1100)    #[must_use]
[1101](https://docs.rs#1101)    fn saturate_fixed(self, amount: Self::Scalar) -> Self;

# Rgb in palette::rgb - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/palette/0.7.6/palette/rgb/struct.Rgb.html

`#[repr(C)]pub struct Rgb<S = `[Srgb](https://docs.rs/encoding/srgb/struct.Srgb.html), T = [f32](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.f32.html)> {
    pub red: T,
    pub green: T,
    pub blue: T,
    pub standard: [PhantomData](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/marker/struct.PhantomData.html)<S>,
}## Expand description

Generic RGB.

RGB is probably the most common color space, when it comes to computer graphics, and it’s defined as an additive mixture of red, green and blue light, where gray scale colors are created when these three channels are equal in strength.

[§](https://docs.rs#creating-a-value)Creating a Value

RGB comes in different shapes and formats. You will probably want to start
with either the [ Srgb](https://docs.rs/type.Srgb.html) or

[alias, which represents the common sRGB format that most images and tools use. Then, depending on your input, you can either just call](https://docs.rs/type.Srgba.html)

`Srgba`[or convert from another data format.](https://docs.rs/struct.Rgb.html#method.new)

`new````
use palette::Srgb;
let rgb_u8 = Srgb::new(171u8, 193, 35);
let rgb_f32 = Srgb::new(0.3f32, 0.8, 0.1);
// `new` is also `const`:
const RGB_U8: Srgb<u8> = Srgb::new(171, 193, 35);
// Converting from one number format to another can be as simple as this:
let rgb_u8_from_f32_1: Srgb<u8> = Srgb::new(0.3f32, 0.8, 0.1).into();
// ...or more explicitly like this:
let rgb_u8_from_f32_2 = Srgb::new(0.3f32, 0.8, 0.1).into_format::<u8>();
// Hexadecimal is also supported, with or without the #:
let rgb_from_hex1: Srgb<u8> = "#f034e6".parse().unwrap();
let rgb_from_hex2: Srgb<u8> = "f034e6".parse().unwrap();
assert_eq!(rgb_from_hex1, rgb_from_hex2);
// This includes the shorthand format:
let rgb_from_short_hex: Srgb<u8> = "f3e".parse().unwrap();
let rgb_from_long_hex: Srgb<u8> = "ff33ee".parse().unwrap();
assert_eq!(rgb_from_short_hex, rgb_from_long_hex);
// It's also possible to convert from (and to) arrays, tuples and `u32` values:
let rgb_from_array = Srgb::from([171u8, 193, 35]);
let rgb_from_tuple = Srgb::from((171u8, 193, 35));
let rgb_from_u32 = Srgb::from(0x607F00);
```
[§](https://docs.rs#linear-srgb-and-gamma-correction)Linear, sRGB and Gamma Correction

Many conversions and operations on RGB require that it’s linear, meaning that gamma correction is required when converting to and from displayable RGB, such as sRGB. It’s common to store and send RGB values where the numbers are on a non-linear scale. In a non-linear format, a value of, for example, 0.5 would not represent a light intensity of 50%, which makes some operations (such as blurring) give incorrect results.

You will probably encounter or use [ LinSrgb](https://docs.rs/type.LinSrgb.html) or

[at some point. These are aliases for linear sRGB and would usually be obtained by converting an](https://docs.rs/type.LinSrgba.html)

`LinSrgba`[value with](https://docs.rs/encoding/srgb/struct.Srgb.html)

`Srgb`[.](https://docs.rs/struct.Rgb.html#method.into_linear)

`into_linear````
use palette::{LinSrgb, Srgb};
// This function uses linear sRGB for something. But how do we interface with it?
fn uses_linear_srgb(input: LinSrgb<f32>) -> LinSrgb<f32> { todo!() }
// Linear sRGB will usually be created from non-linear sRGB:
let output = uses_linear_srgb(Srgb::new(0.3, 0.8, 0.1).into_linear());
// It's also possible to convert directly from u8 to f32 for sRGB.
// This is much faster than using `into_format` first:
let output = uses_linear_srgb(Srgb::new(171u8, 193, 35).into_linear());
// Converting the output back to `Srgb<u8>` (or `Srgb<f32>`) is just as simple:
let output_u8 = Srgb::<u8>::from_linear(output);
// ..or:
let output_u8: Srgb<u8> = output.into_encoding();
```
It’s of course also possible to create a linear value from constants, but
it’s not necessarily as intuitive. It’s best to avoid storing them as
`LinSrgb<u8>` (or `LinRgb<_, u8>`) values, to avoid banding among dark
colors.

See the [ encoding](https://docs.rs/encoding/index.html) module for built-in encoding formats.

[§](https://docs.rs#storage-formats-and-pixel-buffers)Storage Formats and Pixel Buffers

It’s common to read and write RGB values as bytes, hexadecimal strings, or
sometimes `u32` values. A single RGB value can be converted to all of these
formats and more.

```
use palette::{Srgb, LinSrgb};
let source: LinSrgb<f32> = todo!();
let u8_array: [u8; 3] = Srgb::from_linear(source).into();
let hex_string1 = format!("#{:x}", Srgb::<u8>::from_linear(source)); // The # is optional.
let u32_value: u32 = Srgb::from_linear(source).into();
```
It’s also possible to control the component order.
[ PackedArgb](https://docs.rs/type.PackedArgb.html) is one of a few aliases for

[, which represents a color that has been “packed” into a specific data format. This can be a](https://docs.rs/cast/struct.Packed.html)

`Packed``u32` or `[u8; 4]`, for example. This is helpful
for reading and writing colors with a different order than the default RGBA.```
use palette::{rgb::PackedArgb, Srgba, LinSrgba};
let source: LinSrgba<f32> = todo!();
let u8_array: [u8; 4] = PackedArgb::from(Srgba::from_linear(source)).into();
let u32_value: u32 = PackedArgb::from(Srgba::from_linear(source)).into();
```
If you need to work with colors in a byte buffer, such as `[u8]`, `Vec<u8>`
or the `image` crate, there’s a quick way to borrow that buffer as a slice
of RGB(A) colors. The [ cast](https://docs.rs/cast/index.html) module has a number of traits
and functions for casting values without copying them.

```
use image::RgbImage;
use palette::{cast::ComponentsAsMut, Srgb};
let mut image: RgbImage = todo!();
let pixels: &mut [Srgb<u8>] = image.components_as_mut();
for pixel in pixels {
    std::mem::swap(&mut pixel.red, &mut pixel.blue);
}
```

## Implementations[§](https://docs.rs#implementations)

Create an RGB color.

It’s possible to create a color in one number format and convert it to
another format with either [ into_format](https://docs.rs/struct.Rgb.html#method.into_format) or

[.](https://docs.rs/struct.Rgb.html#method.into_linear)

`into_linear````
use palette::{Srgb, LinSrgb};
// Changes only the number format:
let rgb_f32: Srgb<f32> =  Srgb::new(171u8, 193, 35).into_format();
// Changes the number format and converts to linear in one go.
// This is faster than `.into_format().into_linear()`:
let linear: LinSrgb<f32> = Srgb::new(171u8, 193, 35).into_linear();
```

`from_encoding`Convert to a packed `u32` with with specifiable component order.

use palette::{rgb, Srgb};
